speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is frustrating and discouraging to note that there are still some persons and I emphasize "some persons" because the majority are with us inside and outside of this House who have not yet grasped the seriousness of the Quebec situation and who continue to doubt the need for this bill as well as for the emergency measures adopted on October 16. They continue to discuss the situation as if it were an academic exercise, an opportunity for political rhetoric, or a chance to score political points.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) started off by triumphantly stating that "the government has now in effect accepted our leadership in this matter". What does that kind of statement add to a matter as serious as this? If the Leader of the Opposition has truly shown leadership, the Canadian people will recognize it, but I submit that leadership is shown by action and not by words. While the Leader of the Opposition accepted the bill in principle, he repeatedly attempted to pick at the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). One minute he seemed to favour the bill and the next minute he did not. The Canadian people, and in particular the beleaguered people in the province of Quebec, are not concerned at this time with the winning of political or debating points. They expect us here, in Parliament, to take the situation seriously and to work together to find a just and peaceful solution to this problem.
I said there are those who are not convinced of the need for this bill and the emergency measures that were taken. They continue to demand evidence of the apprehended insurrection. For those of us who live in

We, in Montreal, have lived with the evidence and have known it intimately. We have heard the bombs blasting in the mail boxes, we have walked the streets where the blasts took place.

We have heard their hate; we have felt their hostility, and not from a distance, as if we were watching a drama on cinema. We felt it at the St. Jean Baptiste parade riot in 1969, at the McGill Frangais march and at the riots at St. Leonard.

I am not sure of the answer to that question but I do know that this government has been concerned and has tried to act within its powers. There is a very thin line on either side of the question as to whether one goes too far or whether one does too little, but of course that is the problem with which we are dealing. Many people have said we have over reacted, while others have said we have not gone far enough. I say we have been concerned.
I am trying to impress on the House that those of us who live in Montreal and Quebec know at first hand what it is like to live with terror. The Leader of the NDP (Mr. Douglas) has repeatedly stated that the people of
Canada are still waiting for the evidence that the War Measures Act and this bill were necessary. He asked whether we have read the remarks made by Pauline Jewett and Miss LaMarsh and articles which appeared in the Toronto Star as well as those published by the Civil Liberties Union of Canada. He gave us a list of names of people from Toronto, Ottawa and other places, but he mentioned none from Quebec when he spoke yesterday. I should like to ask him whether he has listened to the remarks of Frank Scott, for example, one of the most eminent civil liberties lawyers in Canada or of the "Ligue des Droits d'Hommes" which is the Montreal group concerned with civil liberties, or any Quebec newspapers. Many of these groups and people are not our political partisans. I am not a member of the cabinet and the government might have evidence that I do not have or that I am not aware of, but the evidence that I do have, which is public to all who wish to examine it, is sufficient to my mind to support what the government has done and what the government is doing.
I will repeat this evidence. First of all, we have the expressed intention by the FLQ to engage in terrorist activities including assassination. We have this in their printed literature, which includes instructions on how to create revolution, how to make Molotov cocktails and many other things that are related to violent terrorism. We have also heard these intentions expressed in their speeches. Second, we have information that the FLQ had adequate fire power and personnel to proceed seriously towards its stated goals. Third, we have actual cases where terrorist activities were carried out through bombings, kidnappings, and murders. So, we have their expressed intention in writing and words; we have information that they have the means, and we have cases, in which these intentions have actually been carried out. To me, this is adequate justification for what the government has done.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Nevertheless, some keep asking, where is the revolution? Where is the attempt to overthrow the government? They keep on expecting some type of spectacular uprising, some coup d'etat, some kind of open revolution or civil war. It may be that there is such a plan, but I do not know. It is not what I would expect at this stage. If the FLQ came out in the open to stage that type of uprising or a coup d'etat, they would be easily dealt with; our superior police and armed forces would easily rout and capture them, and the revolution would be finished.
This is not their method. It is not their method even as they describe it in their manual for urban guerilla warfare, or their method as it is carried out in other countries. No, Mr. Speaker, these new revolutionaries hide in their holes and hovels, coming out occasionally to bomb, to kidnap, and to murder at times which best suit their purposes. Their goal is to disrupt society persistently, to keep it off balance, to break its will to continue. This type of urban guerilla warfare is not aimed at the immediate overthrow of the government but at the will of the people to maintain their institutions, their way of life.

It is true that this bill and the regulations introduced on October 16 do limit some civil liberties, but I suggest to you that many others more expert in these matters than I am say this limitation is not very wide.
I attended a teach-in on the present measures with Frank Scott who, as I have already said, is known to be a great civil liberties lawyer, and he stated that the measures that have been introduced are very mild and very limited. As the Prime Minister has said, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has said, nobody really wanted this type of legislation or this type of measure. But, Mr. Speaker, it was the lesser of evils in the situation in which we found ourselves.
We must remember that in democratic societies there is no such thing as unlimited rights. In Quebec, we have the doctrine of "abus de droit", abuse of rights, where one's rights are limited when they come into conflict with the rights of others. In our legal system we have the doctrine of the balance of convenience, through which we allow courts to grant an injunction against the rights of others where we feel there may be a conflict of rights. We insist that the rights of individuals must be limited with respect to the rights of the collectivity, the rights of society.
But let us examine who interfered with civil liberties in what I consider to be a major way. In my opinion, the terror and the violence have been the real cause of restricted liberties in Montreal. Since the commencement of the violence there has been a limit on the liberty of movement enjoyed by the people of Montreal simply because of fear. There has been a serious drop in consumer sales. There has been a cancellation of public social events. Children's events have been cancelled. The children of Montreal no longer may enjoy a Santa Claus parade like children in other Canadian cities. Political meetings in Montreal have been cancelled. There have been many instances where people living in this situation of terror and violence have not been free to do the things that they ordinarily would do if they were not living under such threats.
The new bill before us continues many of the things that were in the regulations, but it removes those parts which were most abhorrent, and it introduces greater protection for those who are accused. The principle object of the bill is to make the FLQ an unlawful association, and those who are members or supporters of it guilty of an offence. Those who are accused under the
Public Order Act, 1970
law will still not have bail unless it is agreed to by the Attorney General, and they still may remain in jail for 90 days before a trial date is set. On the other hand, the period during which they can be held before being charged is reduced from 21 days to seven days.
The measures in the bill are restricted to the FLQ and its successor organizations, which means they cannot be used to weed out and prosecute other types of people who may not be considered desirable by provincial governments, especially governments outside Quebec. The bill provides the right to counsel. It specifically refers to that right, although it is the opinion of the government that that right was not interfered with under the emergency regulations.
Another important provision, with respect to the evidence which can be used to prosecute people under this bill, is the clause which states that a person must have attended several meetings or many meetings of the FLQ, instead of one, before being considered a member of the organization. A serious defect in the regulations under the War Measures Act was the provision that if a person attended even one meeting of the FLQ that fact could be used as evidence against him. The provisions in the regulations dealing with arrest and search without warrant are also continued. To a great extent, the bill is an enactment of the regulations which were made under the War Measures Act.
There has been some discussion about the retroactivity of offences under this bill. Mr. Speaker, I submit that there is no retroactivity of offence under the bill. The offence set out in the bill is that of being a member, or a supporter in various ways, of the FLQ, and that means being a member or supporter after the bill is declared to be in force.
It is true that in the bill there is reference to events, which can be used as evidence, before the bill has come into effect, but these things, of themselves, are not offences. It is not an offence to have attended a meeting or meetings of the FLQ within the past month. Under the bill, it is not an offence to have done things on behalf of the FLQ prior to its introduction and the enactment of the regulations on October 16.
These things raise presumptions against an accused that, as of the day the bill is proclaimed, he is a member of the FLQ. But according to our laws of evidence and legal procedures that presumption can be overturned by casting doubts on it. If a person shows he has taken steps to disassociate himself from the FLQ after the meetings that have been referred to and the evidence brought before the court, then the presumption is rebutted and then the Crown must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the person was a member of the FLQ when the bill was proclaimed. So, the offence is not a retroactive offence. The offence is that of being a member or supporter once the bill comes into effect.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin my remarks this afternoon with two fairly short quotations from a well known Canadian author. They are in French, and are as follows:

As a consequence, when a man is unjustly treated by a given form of authority, all other men are guilty, because they have led the authority to such abuse by their silence and their consent. If they ceased to approve, the authority would fall down.

The second short quotation, particularly for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), is:

Democracy acknowledges that one person may be right and 89 wrong. And this is why in a democracy freedom of speech is deemed sacred: that lone person must always have the right to proclaim his truth in the hope that he can get the 99 others to change their minds.

As hon. members may have guessed if they did not know, these two quotations are from the writings of Pierre Elliott Trudeau and are contained in articles in a weekly called Vrai-True-Published in 1958. They were relevant and right then; they are relevant and right now. It is the man who has changed, and the views of that man have changed. Those of us who stand by the views which he then expressed ought to have at least the ear of people who may disagree instead of the loud, shrill tongue which the Minister of Justice used yesterday. I want to remind hon. members of the House right at the outset that there have already been abuses in the application of the War Measures Act and the regulations under it, great abuses.

As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) informed us, Mr. Speaker, as of today 372 Canadians have been incarcerated, swept into jail, kept there incommunicado from six to 16, to 18 days and then released. In most cases they have been unable to speak with their wives. After the first few days of their incarceration, they were allowed to write a note which the police or some jail guard read to their wives over the telephone. I am not guessing when I say this because I have spoken with quite a few men who were in jail and who came out. According to my information, all of them have been finger printed, photographed and now have a police file. I understand some have lost their jobs. All of them find it difficult to explain to their neighbours and their children why they were incarcerated for days and not interrogated for any more than ten or 15 minutes. Yesterday when I asked the Minister of Justice a question along this line he looked sort of disdainful-I hope he looked as disdainful about the fact that it was done. Those I have spoken to inform me that they were asked questions, the most stupid and irrelevant questions imaginable, that had nothing to do with the situation for which they were arrested and taken out of circulation.
These 372 men and women have no remedy, Mr. Speaker. One of them is a famous singer who has already suffered loss of contracts. There were authors, as well as ordinary workers, but none of these 372 Canadians who suffered this abuse of the law has any recourse or remedy because of the immense and unnecessary power the government insisted on taking on October 16, 1970.

What is wrong with it? It happens to be untrue; the minister knew it and he retracted it as did the Prime Minister. That is what was wrong with the statement. It happens to be untrue. It happens to be true that there were many people in FRAP, most of them having nothing to do with the FLQ, who believed in the democratic process and who entered into the municipal election in Montreal democratically for the purpose of breaking the one party state which now governs Montreal. Anyone who set out to smear this organization, anyone who set out to smear all the people in this organization, has a great deal to account for in terms of proper democratic procedure.
Then, we heard rumours about a plot to upset the government of Quebec. The Prime Minister kept on saying they were rumours. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I know from completely reliable sources that at least two members of the government spoke to other people and told them about this plot before I saw stories in the press. If the Prime Minister does not know this, he can easily find out. It is not for me to name the ministers, but I say on my responsibility as a member of this House that I know from the most reliable sources, the people directly concerned, that at least two ministers spread this rumour long before I saw it in the press.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
Why was this rumour spread? Why did the Prime Minister not deny it when he knew it was not true, that there was no such plot, that there was only a lot of
chit-chat in the editorial of Le Devoir and a lot of chit-chat between Mr. Ryan, Mr. Saulnier and Mr. Bou-rassa? When this matter was raised in the House, the first day, I telephoned Mr. Ryan, Mr. Laberge and Mr. Pepin. I spoke to Mr. Ryan; I could not get the other two gentlemen. He told me what happened, exactly as it appeared in his editorial in Le Devoir last Friday. The Prime Minister knew of these facts. The members of the cabinet knew of these facts. They knew perfectly well that as long as these rumours were allowed to continue, two things would happen. One was that Mr. Ryan and the group of men with him would, in the minds of the rest of Canada, be discredited and seem like traitors. They also knew that if the people in Canada from coast to coast read that there was "a plot to take over the government of Quebec" the only thing they would think about would be the FLQ using force to take over Quebec.
This is what I said over the air. This is what the Minister of Justice took exception to yesterday. I will say it again in this House in his presence, that I believe from the facts that the reason no one in the government denied these rumours about a provisional government was that the government liked the idea that these false rumours were going about because they hoped it would underpin their War Measures Act in the eyes of Canada.

I am tempted to say to the minister that a Liberal preaching intellectual honesty is like a streetwalker preaching virtue. When we said the government was given power under the War Measures Act I always added, and my leader always added, that we knew it was implemented by regulation and that there had been only one regulation. Although I hope the War Measures Act will be withdrawn within a few days, the point I made as long ago as October 16 was that no man should be given the kind of power that the War Measures Act gives. If the act had remained in force, as was the intention of the government, until April 30 next, I shudder to think what other orders in council we might have had, had the situation in certain parts of Canada, in the mind of the government, so required.
My leader explained yesterday the reasons we felt we should vote for this bill on second reading. I agree with the reasons he gave, as do, so far as I know, all my colleagues. But I want to make it clear that, as far as I personally am concerned, I am not entirely convinced that these extended, extraordinary powers are in their totality needed. However, it is the only way we know to get the War Measures Act revoked immediately; certainly, this is what we wish as quickly as possible. It is the only way we know whereby we can bring this bill to committee of the whole and there try to improve it.
I understand that not only members of the opposition but members in the government ranks have some amendments to propose. If the government is going to be adamant in this regard, its action will be entirely inexcusable. If the government insists on retaining the retroactivity provisions in clause 8 of the bill, if it refuses to accept an amendment that seeks to set up what I call a supervisory commission, if it refuses to include in the bill an amendment that I expect a member of the official opposition to present in regard to an independent committee, if it refuses to take away some of these unnecessary powers now contained in the bill, then I will have reason to wonder what it is the government wants, merely power or power for a purpose.
I will suggest in debate in committee of the whole that the bill need not be weakened in the slightest; that it can be improved by interfering less with the civil liberties of people yet be entirely sufficient for the task the bill intends to tackle. We do not weaken the bill when making suggestions from the point of view of its purpose; we seek to improve it from the point of view of the rights and liberties of people. This is why I expect the government to pay attention to what we say.
Since my time is almost up, may I conclude by repeating what I and my leader said on October 16. My reading of history leads me to the conclusion that no group of people consisting of perhaps 30, 50 or 100 men and women only-certainly this is what police work indicates is the size of the group in Quebec-no group of terrorists, can possibly threaten democracy unless social and economic conditions are such that it feels strengthened by the frustration of the young, the despair of the old and

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the speech delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) on Bill C-181, entitled "An Act to provide temporary emergency powers for the preservation of public order in Canada," and I will come back to it later on.
On October 16 last, we were informed of the government's decision to invoke the War Measures Act for the first time in peacetime. On that occasion, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asked the unanimous consent of the House to introduce his motion. He told us that such powers were absolutely necessary to deal with a state of apprehended insurrection in the province of Quebec, following a message received from the Quebec government and the Montreal civic authorities, as reported on page 193 of Hansard.
There was unanimous consent, and the Prime Minister stated precisely the reasons why the government had decided to enforce the War Measures Act. Furthermore, he made it clear that he was truly sorry and deeply worried that the situation called for such action.
Mr. Speaker, I also supported that measure reluctantly, but being convinced it was the only logical step to take in the circumstances, I voted for the enforcement of that act. I am still convinced that this was the only adequate solution left to the government.
The Prime Minister promised the same day, as reported on page 194 of Hansard, and I quote:
Following the passage of enough time to give the government the necessary experience to assess the type of statute which may
be required in these circumstances, it is my firm intention to discuss with the leaders of the opposition parties the desirability of introducing legislation of a less comprehensive nature.
Later on, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) made the same promise. He stated specifically that a new act would be introduced in the House within thirty days.
Mr. Speaker, the minister kept his word and, on November 2, he introduced, to replace the War Measures Act, an act whose short title is Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act, 1970.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice for having kept their word, and I am more proud than ever for being a government member.
The present situation in Canada and more particularly in Quebec is very serious. Let us hope that we shall soon be able to forget that period of our history and pursue together the unification of this country so that it may be the most peaceful in the world.
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to support the government and to vote for that new legislation, for I am still convinced it is not yet time to give ground. We must give the police forces the necessary powers to perform their most important duty, namely to destroy the FLQ once and for all, bring back to Quebec and the whole of Canada peace and quietness and dispell the fear spread by bandits whose aim is to destroy our society.
I am not afraid at all to support that new piece of legislation because I am convinced that should the police arrest innocent people by mistake, they will still be far better in the hands of the police than in- those of the FLQ bandits.
[English}
How does a member of this House feel, Mr. Speaker, when he is confronted with a law such as we were confronted with a short time ago, giving wide powers to our police forces for the first time in Canada's history in peacetime? Like our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and most other members of the House, I abhor violence in all its forms, and dread removing liberties from any citizen, unless it is proven to me that the situation is such that no other way is open to us. That proof was given, Mr. Speaker, and the citizens of Canada by a wide majority supported the government in its decision. Every person in my constituency who either wrote to me on this subject, or spoke to me by telephone or in person, supported the Prime Minister and our government.
No one in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, as far as I know, has lost his or her liberty by our actions, except possibly their own Member of Parliament. Like many other members of this House my residence in the Ottawa area and at Davidson in Pontiac county are under guard by the army, or watched over by the RCMP. As a result, my movements have been restricted and I cannot move about as freely as I have been accustomed to doing. I am quite sure that no one in my family likes the atmosphere created by armed forces personnel standing guard over us. However, Mr. Speaker, I must say that we have found

November 5, 1970

these guards to be perfect gentlemen and very impressive in carrying out their duties. They are a credit to the Armed Forces and to the RCMP. Let us hope that the present situation will soon change and that our family life will return once again to its normal state.
I believe that the new law introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) will give the necessary powers to our police forces in order that they can carry out their duties and, at the same time, protect those persons arrested. Under this bill, persons arrested must be charged within a maximum of seven days rather than the 21 days stipulated in the regulations under the War Measures Act. They will have a right to counsel and jury trial, rights which are not mentioned in the present regulations. Some innocent persons may be picked up and this would be very regrettable, but we must think of our society as a whole, and this new law is the only means by which we can protect the individual as well as our total population in these troubled times.
In supporting this legislation, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to emphasize to my colleagues the importance we must attach to removing the causes for dissatisfaction among some segments of our population. We cannot convert the members of the FLQ because I think they have embarked on a road of no return, but we should show the average citizen in poorer circumstances, who may harbour some sympathy for the FLQ manifesto, that we are taking steps to remedy his situation.
It is an enormous task, but I am convinced that this government can do it with the co-operation of all hon. members in the House, and that all the citizens of our country will reap the benefits. The Minister of Justice, who made a brilliant speech yesterday on this bill, explained why new measures are needed to combat new problems as they arise in our ever-changing society. We must meet this challenge, Mr. Speaker, and meet it now. Canada has perhaps lost her innocence, as the Minister of Justice said. I am convinced, however, that she has not lost her wisdom and her determination to bring about the just society. The legally elected government of Quebec and the municipal government of Montreal concurred in a request that special measures be taken. The federal government accepted their request and proclaimed the War Measures Act.

Let us hope that even this new act will never be proclaimed again; but let us forever be ready to invoke it if the need arises. The Canadian people have the right to expect and demand this of us, and our duty is to accept it and fulfil our mandate for Canada.

Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a suggestion to the cabinet. I wish that more funds be appropriated for the economic development of underdeveloped areas. We will thus contribute greatly to improve the living conditions and to decrease

After hearing the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) flinging abuse at the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) and at the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), perhaps I am entitled to take at least a few minutes and reply to such nonsense.

The Secretary of State blamed the member for Temiscamingue for wanting to bring before the firing squad the FLQ leaders who apparently remain unknown only to the government.
If an attempt by some individuals to overthrow a government by the means we know is not what is commonly called treason, I do not know what it is. I myself sometimes wonder if the present government is not satisfied with the situation and if in a sense it did not bring about the present conditions in Canada.

There are precedents with regard to sedition. In 1918, one Mr. Russell, informally recognized as a Communist, because there was no Communist party at that time, made seditious remarks during public meetings. I will quote one which he made at the Walker theatre on December 22, 1918, as reported in the book from which I quoted a moment ago:
Blood is shed in Russia and it will be shed also in Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, or else we will get our rights. We will not hesitate to walk in blood in order to obtain what we believe are our rights.
Mr. Speaker, Russell was found guilty of sedition after that statement.
For years, and mainly in the province of Quebec, statements have been made at least as seditious as Russell's in 1918. Nevertheless, nothing has been done about it. I wonder why we always wait until the last minute to do something.
The bill now under study is designed to replace the War Measures Act which it has been necessary to proclaim because of the October events in Quebec. In fact, it was necessary to put this act into force because of Mr. Cross's and Laporte's kidnappings and because of the sadistic murder of the latter on October 16.

What should one think about the innocents who are threatened? I appreciate the fact that hon. members who live in the shadow of the Rockies may find it difficult to read the Quebec newspapers; nevertheless they could come closer to that province, where the crisis is the most obvious at the present time, by reading the newspapers and by consulting with their colleagues here, regardless of their party affiliation to find out what is really happening in our province.
There is much talk about civil liberties but the victims are forgotten. There are many of them at the present time. I think of Cross, Laporte and other innocent people who are threatened. I think of the citizens of Montreal who are afraid even to go to the movies at night. I think of those who have stopped going to night clubs. I think of those who must abstain from attending social or political events of all kinds. That is what is going on in the province of Quebec. Perhaps that in the shadows of the Rockies they are not aware of it right now but I hope that such tragic events never happen there. Today it is FLQ but maybe later on it will be the FLBC-

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Why are you filibustering your own bill?

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Children in schools, in CEGEPs, in universities, are threatened by other children who incite them to resort to blackmail, even though their parents make every effort to educate them properly. Here is an example: The hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and myself went to the University of Sherbrooke to explain federalism to the students. By the way, the second issue, first volume, of the Estrien Rouge, published in the province of Quebec on April 3, 1970, with a picture of Mao on the front page and sold for 10 cents, contained, as the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) reported previously, the following which I quote:
The stand taken by those traitors, Ouellet and Gervais, who represent the colonialists, clearly proves that only the power of the people can drive them out of Quebec.

And then, it will be argued that there was not sufficient evidence to proclaim the War Measures Act.
I think that perhaps the time has come to proceed with the study of the bill and to stop rehashing old stories, as we did this afternoon. The aim of this bill is to extend the powers of the Attorneys General or of the Minister of Justice, as we say in the province of Quebec, those powers being delegated to the police forces in order to allow them to work more efficiently.
Those who claim that civil liberties are impaired will not approve, of course, in principle, a special act but taking into account the present context and such a complex situation, I do not think that it is so restrictive.
There is the matter of bail, of arrest, search and seizure without warrant. But, on the other hand, if one refers to the preamble of the bill now under consideration, one can see that if an individual has done nothing wrong, he has nothing to be afraid of.
Some people are acting out of political expediency, such as our friends from the New Democratic Party, who do not really know Quebec-there is not even one in the House who represents a riding from that province-but they could have consulted us. Anyway, the vote was eloquent enough to show them that other members were perhaps more enlightened than they were. In spite of these facts, I suspect they are not aware of the situation and after discussions, telephone conversations with people from other provinces, I submit that these members do not even represent the views of their constituents.
The people of Canada almost unanimously, support action taken by the government since the emergency measures have been in force.
As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has pointed out, there might be some abuse in the application of the legislation. That is unfortunate, but in the present circumstances we must apply it, and it is the responsibility of the Attorney General or the Minister of Justice of the province to see that the law is observed and that arbitrary measures are curbed to the greatest possible extent.
Others criticise the government for not having acted soon enough, as the previous speaker said. I should have liked to see how the same people would have reacted had the government taken action, say six months or a year ago. What would have been their attitude, had the government taken action before the kidnappings, before the assassination of Mr. Laporte, before the violent deaths caused by acts of terrorism? Then there would have been a terrible filibuster. The government would have been accused of taking fascist measures, whereas today we must act in that delicate and painful situation we have now.
In Canada we were not prepared to face a situation such as this one. The events followed in rapid succession whereas we were accustomed to live in an orderly way, in peace and in tranquillity. As they say in English: "We were smug, we felt smug." Unfortunately to defend one's liberty it is necessary to accept sacrifices and restrictions
November 5, 1970

of that liberty. It is in this spirit that the bill is introduced.
As for those who will say that there was no reason for proclaiming the War Measures Act, I answer them by quoting some excerpts from a document submitted to the committee which inquired into the Company of Young Canadians last summer:

Inevitably, Quebec revolutionaries will come to group themselves in a single movement without, however, losing their own identities.
That they fight today in the FLP, the FLQ, the citizen's committees, the MLT, the MIS, the Vallieres-Gagnon committee, and the unions makes little difference. They all participate in the same strategy.
There are not 50 strategies. There are only two: electoral and revolutionary strategy.
Is this not evidence, gentlemen? I will go on.

Here in Quebec the fight for the destruction of the capitalist system is inseparable from the struggle for national independence. One will not go far without the other.
Another quotation from the same article reads as follows:
Plan of Action: In the immediate future we must continue and increase the agitation, propaganda and permanent contestation at all levels of society so we can unmask, expose, demystify and weaken the cogwheels of the system which imprisons workers and students in stifling slavery.
Excellent work has already been done in this area; it must continue-
Inevitably this will lead to violence and breaking the law. But it is absolutely normal for a revolutionary to operate outside the law-
The FLQ Manifesto ends this way:
It is easier than denouncing the system, easier than protesting, to make the FLQ a convenient scapegoat for everyone.
But one must remember that it is all Quebec revolutionaries who, through their actions and determination, have brought forth the FLQ.
And the FLQ will endure as long as there are revolutionaries in Quebec who are determined to conquer.
There again, if some hon. members suspect that there is no evidence, I could give them more literature in private.

Like the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), I agree that the enforcement of this bill obviously will not kill terrorism once and for all, but it will provide the Minister of Justice of the province of Quebec with an instrument which will enable him and his police forces to carry on their investigations and arrest this pack of criminals.
The mere mention of some crimes in the Criminal Code will not eliminate them but, on the other hand, our police forces are thus empowered to rid our society of criminals.
Public Order Act, 1970
Mr. Speaker, in closing, let me say that we must all support this piece of legislation and instead of indulging in sarcasm and being nasty to our police officers, our duty is to offer them whatever co-operation and support we can provide in order that we may once again find this atmosphere which we long for and cherish heartily.

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Little or no argument can be raised against the proposition that every civil right that we enjoy is subject to the supremacy of Parliament. Parliament has jurisdiction over all civil rights. Acting within the scope of its authority and according to the exigencies of the situation which face the nation, province or municipality at the time, it is the supremacy of Parliament that counts. There is no such thing as an absolute civil right. There is no such thing as the right to liberty that is not subject to the supremacy of Parliament. There is no such thing as the right to security of the person and the right to the enjoyment of property. Any of these rights can be taken away by the due process of law. That is expressly stated in the Bill of Rights. It is something that Canadians should not forget.
The right to equality before the law, protection of the law, freedom of relig'on, speech, assembly, association and of the press are all subject to abrogation, variation and change by the process of law.

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
The due process of law can mean the passage of a statute such as the one we are discussing today, an order of a court of an appropriate jurisdiction, or a regulation passed pursuant to authority delegated to the Governor in Council by Parliament, such as happened with the War Measures Act.
It has been suggested that the War Measures Act has just been proclaimed. In fact, it was proclaimed in 1914. It has been on the statute books ever since, and now we are merely acting under it. To suggest that we acted with the full force and effect of the act is absolute nonsense. The only right which approaches an absolute civil right is the right to habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari or the right to prohibition. None of these rights have been abridged by the regulations under the War Measures Act or the bill with which we are now dealing.

speechtext:
There will be charges. It is provided in the regulations and the bill before us. We live in changing times, Mr. Speaker. It is time we realized that we live in very troubled times. We can no longer put our heads in the sand. We live in a world where the old values, the status quo and authoritarianism of the past are rapidly being replaced by concepts which have yet to be truly formalized and structured into acceptable political philosophy.

The people in our community today have been emancipated by superior education. They are knowledgeable by virtue of the vast progress that has been made in the field of mass communication. They are conscious as never before of the needless poverty in our country, the decadence and the intolerable bureaucracy with which we are faced at all levels of government. Young people in particular are testing and rejecting many of the concepts which the authoritarians cling to like a young baby clings to a tattered baby blanket. They have had enough. Such testing can by no means be considered to be among only the young people. There are many adults who have seen a little bit of everything, experienced a little bit of everything and seen the slowness of it. We see how long it takes to have the most minor reforms passed in this House. There was a 16-day filibuster on the omnibus bill dealing with abortion. There were 16 days of nothing but talk, the same thing over and over again. The reactionary forces are holding fast; the activists and reformists are anxious to get ahead.

speechtext: The bill was the only abortion.

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: I will tell you about that in a moment.

speechtext: I did not ask you that.

maintopic: PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
In encouraging dialogue, encouraging young people to get into the political institutions which we represent, and encouraging them to make changes we must have a peaceful transition and reform. In a rebellious world there is no room for violence. We cannot tolerate violence. When a government fails to act, refuses to change and refuses to see the causes of violence in its community, there is every chance the extremists, megalomaniacs and psychopaths will become terrorists. To a large extent, this is what happened in our community today.
This is not the occasion to discuss long-term solutions for what has happened. It is not the occasion to consider what has happened in our universities, among the working people, the unemployed and our ethnic groups such as the Metis who are dissatisfied. Today is not the time to discuss this, but it must be discussed soon. Nor is it a time to dwell on transformation and change of the government. It is not the time to blame, accuse or confront. We all carry, in a sense, a certain amount of the blame. What we must consider today is the legislation before us, its necessity, its provisions and hopeful effect. Regardless of what might have been said about rumours of the takeover of the government of Quebec, in my view there was ample evidence upon which this government and the province of Quebec were entitled to act, not only entitled but obligated to act to preserve social order. I am only surprised that we acted with the restraint with which we did.
Much has been said to the effect that the government had no basis and no ground on which to introduce regulations under the War Measures Act and that there was no evidence of apprehended insurrection. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has said that we should
November 5, 1970

have acted earlier and taken effective action. These are two points I would like to discuss. Obviously, before October 16 we did not have a request for assistance from the government of Quebec. The government of the province of Quebec did not write to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asking for such powers. Hon. members will recall in hearings before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts that this matter was dealt with. There was never a request from the Government of Quebec for assistance.
Does the Leader of the Opposition suggest that the government of Canada should have acted in the absence of such a request? Should we have demonstrated that the government of the province of Quebec had no power to enforce the law in that province? That is contrary to the Constitution. Surely, it was the request of Mr. Bourassa and others, coupled with other evidence, that brought about the invocation of the regulations under the War Measures Act. Should the federal government have refused to act when the Premier of the province of Quebec requested assistance?
Consider the facts which we have heard. I will deal with them very briefly. In the last ten years we have witnessed bombings, we have witnessed riots, obviously organized, in the city of Montreal. There have been crimes of murder extending even to the city of Ottawa, last June. There have been robberies so that these people could gain their financial ends. There have been thefts of dynamite, thefts of weapons.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Hon. members can read today in the Globe and Mail about the discovery of a cache of weapons including carbines, machine-guns and a bazooka. Mr. Speaker, these are not for shooting ducks. They were to be used for one purpose only, and that is to destroy the social order. Twenty-three persons are in jail as a result of crimes perpetrated in the name of political power. If we can attribute these acts to the FLQ and its related associations, in these circumstances it would appear to me that we have been modest in our actions.
Consider the evidence which was produced before the Committee on Broadcasting last year. We heard about the infiltration of terrorists into the Company of Young Canadians. We were told by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) in that committee that we were not to go on a witch-hunt, that we were confined in our terms of reference to dealing with the CYC. No request was made by the government of Quebec for assistance at that time. We heard from Mr. Saulnier, we heard from Mr. Cote. They were convinced then that there were grounds for apprehending an insurrection; not the next day, but they said it was coming, it was on its way. And they showed us the documentation which had been seized throughout the city of Montreal, obviously designed for distribution throughout the whole of Quebec. Since 1963, ever since the explosion of the first FLQ bombs, we have been in that first stage of the revolutionary struggle which will be pursued until agitation becomes widespread and culminates in a general political, social and economic crisis. We are now approaching this crisis very rapidly, and this has been particularly the case in the last six months.
It goes on:
This is the sort of struggle which is conducted daily, each according to his means, by the FLP, MIS, FLQ et cetera. This many sided action, which pursues the same objectives everywhere, is dominated by propaganda, agitation, ideological training of militants, and the progressive organization at the basic levels, of active cells, whether it be FLP cells, citizens' committees, political action unions, committees, strike committees, clandestine and armed FLQ cells, et cetera.
I do not intend to go through all this evidence tonight, but there is ample documentation here to show that the FLQ did plan an insurrection. Passages in these documents explained how to make Molotov cocktails, how to put ball-bearings beneath the feet of horses in a riot so that the police forces would stumble, how to use military weapons, machine-guns, carbines and the like, how to protect oneself with safety devices against anti-riot equipment. This clearly showed the purport of the FLQ.
It might be said that the committee dealt lightly with this evidence, that its members buried their heads in the sand. But, I repeat, there was no request on the part of the government of Quebec at that time for any action in this field. But the kidnappings of Mr. Cross and Mr. Laporte were obviously the last straw; it was obviously indicative to the government of Quebec, with the totality of its police force engaged in trying to apprehend those who had committed these acts, that the existing measures

November 5, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
governing law enforcement were inadequate. It was obvious that special powers were required, and they decided to act. It could not be said that insurrection was about to take place, because nobody knew. But, certainly, it was properly apprehended in the true sense because all these acts were committed pursuant to the basic manifesto, parts of which I have read out-a manifesto which indicated that at some future date, very soon, an insurrection might take place.
The action of the government, directed to stopping this terror, has been to sweep up all those suspected of any connection with it. I agree that this is an infringement of the civil rights usually enjoyed by Canadians. I do not like it. It required an awful lot of soul-searching to conclude it was necessary. But when one considers the overall picture, the fact that the Bourassa government is a young government, a government which had yet, really, to formulate its policy, it is apparent that the action we took was absolutely necessary and justified in the circumstances. The whole pattern indicates a format of insurrection, and if hon. members opposite cannot see that I suggest to them, with the greatest respect, that they are blind. This bill is quite moderate, considering what it might be.

speechtext: It is fair and it is just. I repeat my statement. A government acting in panic would surely have imposed censorship. The suggestion that there are retroactive provisions in the bill are not well-founded. Any experienced lawyer will confirm this. It is only the circumstances surrounding proof which are given retroactive effect. In the last analysis, the burden of proof remains upon the Crown. The Crown must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. I should like to hear some of the lawyers in the opposition discuss the question of rebuttable presumption and what happens to the burden of proof. It does not change. Within 90 days a trial date has to be fixed. I am not too sure I would not rather be charged under this bill than under the Criminal Code, because under the Code there is no obligation to fix a date for trial within 90 days.

When I am through. We have to find the cause. It is clear to me, as it must be clear to all hon. members, that as long as we encourage dissent, as we do by participatory democracy and the like, we have to be more conscious than ever before of the security of this nation. We must have some introspection at all levels of government in future programs. We must consider changes in the criminal law dealing with group liability, sedition, treason and the like. We must be able to erase the basic structure upon which terrorists rely for their support in riots, and so on. We must consider our traditional concept of civil rights in a changing society and give it very close scrutiny. Greater freedom means greater responsibility. We have to examine civil rights in the light of a changing world.
I am satisfied that we can solve these problems in the future. I agree with the government that now is not the time to introduce such long-range, profound and deep legislation pertaining to civil rights. If we take our time in the sense of studying the question during this session of Parliament, hopefully we can come up with something that will be beneficial to the people of Canada in years to come.

many critics have charged that his selection lacked depth, profundity and musical integrity; and that while this harsh melody might be on everyone's lips for the moment, there was no real evidence to conclude that its popularity could prevail for long, in spite of the cleverness of its construction and the elaborate polyphony of its texture, and finally, that it would certainly never stand the test of history as a masterpiece orchestrated, as it was, by the Department of Public Works.
Other critics agree that the whole composition was a badly balanced one from a structural point of view. The pianissimo introduction, though pedestrian, was lulling enough to suit most tastes. After such an extended development section the coda, naturally, was awaited anxiously by all. When it came, an immense gasp of relief was heard from the audience, undoubtedly because, as in common with all audiences, this one identified with and shared the embarrassment of the soloist. A minor aside really, Mr. Speaker, but apparently the percussion section members were not paying sufficient attention to their scores, because many players tended to proceed with the rythmic ostinato long after it was quite plain to everyone else that the piece had ended.
I would like to turn at this point and give some attention to the technique displayed by the French horn soloist, the Minister of Justice. It was quite evident that yesterday's concert did not rank with his best. While the listeners had little reason to expect virtuosity from him, it saddens me to say that at least they could expect virtue. Perhaps serious music is not the best field for the talents of this young man. With his inborn personal attractiveness and his carefully acquired charm, he might do extremely well in the pop field. Others have abandoned classics for pop with no discredit to them. I mention only two to support my thesis, Xavier Cugat, who was once concert master for the New York Philharmonic, and Lome Greene, who forsook Shakespeare for "Bonanza."
I think that in discussing technical matters it would only be fair and kindly to point out to the minister that delicate nuances of tone capable of being produced by the French horn are better accomplished by the player inserting just his right hand rather than his whole right wing into the bell of this delicate instrument. Perhaps, though, this extravagant employment of the right wing was a not so subtle appeal to the nostalgia of the good old days when people were offered less dissonance, and a total acceptance of what was musically good prevailed throughout the land.
It must be said, too, that I was extremely disappointed by the way in which the performer handled the relatively simple triple-tongueing passages in the cadenza. Most agree that this particular soloist is superbly equipped for triple-tongueing and has displayed this ability remarkably on numerous previous occasions. Yesterday, alas, was not his day.
Typically, however, his reliance on the staccato style remains unimpaired. A series of short, detached bursts followed by deep-furrowed silences-believed to indicate thinking-have been a trademark of the minister's style for some years. Musicologists have theorize that his delivery has developed over many years in a valiant effort to overcome a childhood impediment caused by his efforts to speak clearly without the necessity of removing the silver spoon.
To conclude, let me say that regardless of what field of musical endeavour the soloist might find in the future satisfying and rewarding, it is obvious to me that he has directed far too much of his studies exclusively to the works patronized in aristocratic chambers. It is this critic's view that the soloist would do better to develop a greater acquaintanceship with composers such as Sibelius, Aaron Copland, or even the Beatles who have used as a stimulus for their creativity the melodies reflecting aspirations of little men living in a free society. And above all he must remember that when playing the French horn the best results by far are achieved if one keeps a stiff upper lip at all times.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make one of my shortest speeches in this House, for which many members may be thankful. I rise merely to say that I feel this House is on the verge of committing itself to legislation that is very much against the best interests of this country. I will not go into all the arguments that I raised on October 16 and 17 when we discussed the War Measures Act, but they would apply equally to the legislation that is before us tonight. What we are dealing with is, in effect, just a revised standard version of the War Measures Act regulations. For that reason I have decided to place my vote against these regulations and against this new act.
I am sure that many people will recall that I supported the move of the government on October 18 or 19 to enforce the War Measures Act and its regulations. I did so, not without a great deal of thought and with some uncertainty on my part but basically in good faith, believing that the government had rightly apprehended the situation as it existed in the province of Quebec and was taking what at that time seemed to be a reasonable step. I now believe, 2 1/2 weeks later, that step to have been unwise and one that I can no longer support.
I cannot support this legislation and I certainly cannot support the War Measures Act. I will, as a member of this House, use every opportunity that I have to see it removed as quickly as possible. I think what we have done to the country has been amply proven here in the last few days by the kind of intemperate remarks, most of them irrelevant, and the fact that we have not been given, even to this day, sufficient justification either inside or outside the House to warrant the government asking for and producing the kind of legislation that I feel will, and has, very detrimentally affected this country.

November 5, 1970
